p1.title: Part 1 · Solid-State Materials and Intrinsic Carriers
p1.intro: Electronic materials fall into three categories based on their resistivity (ρ). The resistivity of a semiconductor can be controlled by adding impurity atoms to the crystal.
p1.li1: Elemental semiconductors are formed from a single type of atom in column IV of the periodic table; compound semiconductors combine elements from columns III and V or II and VI.
p1.li2: Germanium was used in many early devices. Silicon replaced it thanks to its higher bandgap, lower cost and the ease of growing an insulating SiO<sub>2</sub> layer.
p1.li3: A Si atom has 4 electrons in its outer shell. Each atom forms covalent bonds with its 4 nearest neighbors, creating a regular diamond lattice. Single crystal material is the most useful for electronics.
p1.li4: At 0 K all bonds are complete and Si behaves as an insulator. As temperature rises, some bonds break and electron-hole pairs are generated.
p1.niText: E<sub>G</sub>: bandgap energy (eV), k = 8.62×10<sup>-5</sup> eV/K, T: absolute temperature (K), B = 1.08×10<sup>31</sup> K<sup>-3</sup>cm<sup>-6</sup> (Si). At room temperature n<sub>i</sub> ≈ 10<sup>10</sup> cm<sup>-3</sup> for silicon.
p1.li5: An electron leaving a bond leaves behind a vacancy with charge +q, called a hole. Hole density is written as p.
p1.li6: For intrinsic silicon n = ni = p. In thermal equilibrium, pn = ni2.
p1.driftText: For intrinsic Si, μ<sub>n</sub> = 1350 and μ<sub>p</sub> = 500 cm<sup>2</sup>/V·s. Hole mobility is lower because hole current involves multiple covalent bond disruptions. Example: at room temperature intrinsic Si has conductivity σ = 2.96×10<sup>-6</sup> (Ω·cm)<sup>-1</sup> and resistivity ρ = 3.38×10<sup>5</sup> Ω·cm, so intrinsic silicon is a poor insulator.

p2.title: Part 2 · Doping, Drift and Diffusion
p2.intro: Doping is adding very small, well-controlled amounts of impurities to a semiconductor. For silicon, impurities come from columns III and V.
p2.donorText: Column V atoms such as phosphorus, arsenic and antimony. With five outer electrons, the atom brings one extra electron that needs very little energy to become free. The ionized donor atom has a fixed charge of +q.
p2.acceptorText: Column III atoms such as boron. An incomplete bond, i.e. a hole, is created. A nearby electron easily moves into the vacancy and the hole travels like a particle. The ionized acceptor has a fixed charge of −q.
p2.f1: Charge neutrality: q(N<sub>D</sub> + p − N<sub>A</sub> − n) = 0    pn = n<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>
p2.li1: At practical doping levels (10<sup>14</sup> ≤ |N<sub>A</sub>−N<sub>D</sub>| ≤ 10<sup>21</sup> cm<sup>-3</sup>) we can take n ≈ N<sub>D</sub>−N<sub>A</sub> or p ≈ N<sub>A</sub>−N<sub>D</sub>.
p2.li2: Majority carrier concentration is set during manufacturing and is independent of temperature. Minority carriers are proportional to ni2 and are therefore strongly temperature dependent.
p2.li3: Doping degrades mobility: impurity atoms scatter the carriers. As total doping N<sub>T</sub> = N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>D</sub> increases, mobility drops rapidly.
p2.diffText: Carriers move from regions of high concentration to regions of low concentration, just like a gas spreading across a room.
p2.f2: Einstein relation: D<sub>n</sub>/μ<sub>n</sub> = D<sub>p</sub>/μ<sub>p</sub> = kT/q = V<sub>T</sub> ≈ 25 mV (thermal voltage)

p3.title: Part 3 · Energy Band Model
p3.li1: The conduction band and valence band are the allowed energy states for electrons.
p3.li2: EV: top edge of the valence band. EC: bottom edge of the conduction band. The difference is the bandgap EG.
p3.li3: At 0 K all electrons are in the valence band and no conduction occurs. At T > 0 K thermal energy breaks bonds, electrons move up to the conduction band and holes appear in the valence band.
p3.li4: The donor level ED is very close to EC (about 0.045 eV for phosphorus).
p3.li5: The acceptor level EA is very close to EV (about 0.044 eV for boron).
p3.li6: A compensated semiconductor contains both n-type and p-type dopants. If ND > NA, donor electrons fill the acceptor sites and the remaining ND−NA electrons can move up to the conduction band.

s3p1.intro: A diode is formed by joining an n-type semiconductor with a p-type semiconductor. The interface between the two regions is the pn junction (metallurgical junction). The p side is the anode and the n side is the cathode.
s3p1.f1: p side: p<sub>p</sub> = N<sub>A</sub> , n<sub>p</sub> = n<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>/N<sub>A</sub>     n side: n<sub>n</sub> = N<sub>D</sub> , p<sub>n</sub> = n<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>/N<sub>D</sub>
s3p1.li1: The carrier concentrations differ enormously across the junction (e.g. 1017 holes/cm3 on the p side versus 104 on the n side). These gradients drive diffusion: holes move from p to n and electrons move from n to p.
s3p1.li2: Each hole leaving the p side leaves behind an immobile, negatively charged ionized acceptor; each electron leaving the n side leaves behind a positively charged ionized donor. The carrier-free region around the junction is the depletion region, or space charge region (SCR).
s3p1.li3: The fixed charge produces an electric field pointing from n to p, and this field gives rise to a drift current that opposes diffusion.
s3p1.li4: In an open-circuited diode drift and diffusion cancel exactly and the net current is zero. No actual current flows, since that would imply power dissipation; the field simply cancels the diffusion tendency.
s3p1.elec: The space charge density is −qNA on the p side (from −xp to 0) and +qND on the n side (from 0 to xn). Because the total charge on the two sides must be equal, the depletion region extends further into the more lightly doped side. The electric field is the integral of the charge density: zero outside the depletion region and maximum (EMAX) at the junction.
s3p1.builtin: The built-in potential φj is the voltage developed across the junction by the field; it represents a barrier to electron and hole flow. It equals the area under the triangular E(x) plot. εs = 11.7ε0, ε0 = 8.85×10-14 F/cm.
s3p1.ex1: Example: for NA = 1017 cm-3, ND = 1020 cm-3 and VT = 0.025 V we get φj = 0.979 V, wd0 = 0.113 µm, xp = 0.113 µm, xn = 1.13×10-4 µm and EMAX = 2φj/wd0 = 173 kV/cm. Nearly all of the depletion region lies on the lightly doped p side. Sanity check: the built-in potential should be less than the bandgap of silicon (1.12 V).
s3p1.eq: IS: reverse saturation current (typically 10-18 to 10-9 A and strongly temperature dependent through ni2), vD: voltage applied to the diode, n: nonideality factor (assumed to be 1 here), VT = kT/q: thermal voltage (≈ 25 mV at room temperature).
s3p1.bias: Biasing means applying a dc voltage to a device. The diode equation has three cases:
s3p1.li5: The turn-on voltage marks the point of significant current flow (roughly 0.6–0.7 V for silicon).
s3p1.li6: In forward bias a voltage increase of about 60 mV raises the current by a factor of 10: ΔvD = VT·ln10 ≈ 57.6 mV.
s3p1.li7: In practice the reverse leakage current is larger than I<sub>S</sub> and increases gradually with reverse voltage, so these expressions are approximations.
s3p1.ex2: Example: for IS = 0.1 fA and ID = 300 µA, VD = nVT·ln(1 + ID/IS) = 0.718 V. With IS = 10 fA the result is 0.603 V; with ID = 1 mA it is 0.748 V.
s3p1.temp: V<sub>GO</sub> is the silicon bandgap voltage at 0 K (1.12 V). At constant current, the forward voltage of a diode decreases by about 1.8 mV for each 1 °C increase in temperature.
s3p1.title: Part 1 · The pn Junction and the Diode Equation

s3p2.intro: When an external voltage is applied to the diode, essentially all of it drops across the space charge region. The barrier at the junction becomes φj − vD, which disturbs the balance between the drift and diffusion currents.
s3p2.li1: A reverse voltage vR (vD = −vR) adds to the built-in potential: the barrier becomes φj + vR, and majority carriers can no longer cross the junction.
s3p2.li2: The larger electric field must be supported by additional charge, so the depletion region widens. Its width increases in proportion to the square root of the applied reverse voltage.
s3p2.is: The reverse current results from thermal generation of electron-hole pairs in the depletion region, so it depends on the volume of the space charge region and increases gradually with reverse bias. Under forward bias the width changes very little and IS ≈ IS0.
s3p2.ex1: Example: for a diode with wd0 = 0.4 µm and φj = 0.85 V, doubling the width requires 1 + vR/φj = 4, i.e. vR = 3φj = 2.55 V. At a reverse bias of 5 V, wd = 0.4·√(1 + 5/0.85) = 1.05 µm.
s3p2.bd: Increasing the reverse bias eventually drives the diode into the breakdown region, where the diode current rises sharply. The voltage at which this occurs is the breakdown voltage VZ (2 V ≤ VZ ≤ 2000 V). There are two mechanisms:
s3p2.avText: As the electric field increases, accelerated carriers collide with fixed atoms and ionize them (impact ionization). The new carriers also accelerate and ionize other atoms, so the process feeds on itself. The breakdown voltage increases with temperature.
s3p2.zText: Occurs in heavily doped diodes, where the depletion region is very narrow. Carriers tunnel directly between the valence and conduction bands. The breakdown voltage decreases with temperature.
s3p2.zmodel: In breakdown the diode is modeled by a voltage source VZ in series with a small resistance RZ (< 100 Ω). Diodes designed to operate in reverse breakdown are called Zener diodes. The sign of the temperature coefficient is a quick way to distinguish the two mechanisms.
s3p2.li3: Reverse bias (junction capacitance Cj): a change in voltage changes the charge in the depletion region, which gives the diode a capacitance. Cj decreases as the reverse-bias voltage increases. A diode optimized as a voltage-controlled capacitor is called a varactor.
s3p2.li4: Forward bias (diffusion capacitance CD): additional charge is stored in the neutral regions near the edges of the space charge region. It is proportional to the diode current; τT is the diode transit time. CD becomes quite large at high currents.
s3p2.schottky: Replacing one semiconductor region of the pn diode with a non-ohmic rectifying metal contact on n-type silicon gives a Schottky diode; the metal region is the anode. It turns on at a lower voltage than a pn junction diode and has significantly reduced charge storage under forward bias.
s3p2.title: Part 2 · Reverse Bias, Breakdown and Capacitance

s3p3.m1: Plot the load line on the i-v characteristic; the intersection is the Q-point.
s3p3.m2: Substitute the diode equation into the loop equation and solve numerically.
s3p3.m3: On: short circuit (v<sub>D</sub> = 0). Off: open circuit (i<sub>D</sub> = 0).
s3p3.m4: On: a voltage source V<sub>on</sub> = 0.6 V. Off: open circuit.
s3p3.intro: The objective of diode circuit analysis is to find the quiescent operating point, or Q-point = (ID, VD), of the diode. V and R below may represent the Thévenin equivalent of a more complex two-terminal network.
s3p3.methods: Because the relationship between I<sub>D</sub> and V<sub>D</sub> is nonlinear, this equation cannot be solved on its own. There are four approaches; the results below are for V = 10 V and R = 10 kΩ:
s3p3.digits: All four methods give nearly the same current. Since accurate saturation current values are rarely available and sources and passive components have significant tolerances, answers precise to two or three significant digits are sufficient.
s3p3.li1: Two points define the load line: ID = V/R = 1 mA at VD = 0 and ID = 0.5 mA at VD = 5 V. Its slope is −1/R. The Q-point is the intersection of the load line with the diode i-v characteristic.
s3p3.li2: Mathematical model: for IS = 10-15 A, n = 1 and VT = 0.025 V the loop equation becomes 10 = 104·10-15[exp(40VD) − 1] + VD. This is a transcendental equation; a numerical answer is found by trial and error or Newton's iterative method.
s3p3.h2: Analysis steps with the ideal and CVD models
s3p3.st2: Identify the anode and cathode of the diode and label v<sub>D</sub> and i<sub>D</sub>.
s3p3.st3: Guess the diode's region of operation from the circuit.
s3p3.st4: Analyze the circuit using the model appropriate for the assumed region of operation.
s3p3.st5: Check the results for consistency with the assumption: iD > 0 if on, vD < 0 if off (vD < Von for the CVD model). If they are inconsistent, change the assumption and try again.
s3p3.ex1: Example (two diodes, ideal model): a +15 V source feeds node D through 10 kΩ. D1 connects node D to ground and D2 connects node D through 5 kΩ to −10 V. Assuming both diodes are on, node D is at 0 V: I1 = 15/10k = 1.5 mA, ID2 = 10/5k = 2 mA and ID1 = 1.5 − 2 = −0.5 mA. A negative diode current is not allowed, so the assumption is wrong. Assuming D1 off and D2 on gives ID2 = 25 V / 15 kΩ = 1.67 mA and VD1 = 15 − 10k·1.67 mA = −1.67 V, which is consistent: D1 = (0 mA, −1.67 V) off, D2 = (1.67 mA, 0 V) on.
s3p3.pwl: A diode in breakdown is analyzed with the piecewise linear model: a source VZ in series with RZ. Example: for a 20 V source, a 5 kΩ resistor, VZ = 5 V and RZ = 100 Ω, IZ = (20 − 5)/5100 = 2.94 mA and the voltage across the diode is 5 + 2.94 mA·100 Ω = 5.29 V. Since IZ > 0, the solution is consistent with Zener breakdown.
s3p3.reg: A Zener diode connected in parallel with the load keeps the voltage across the load constant. This circuit is a voltage regulator:
s3p3.li3: Example: for V<sub>S</sub> = 20 V, R = 5 kΩ, V<sub>Z</sub> = 5 V and R<sub>L</sub> = 5 kΩ: I<sub>S</sub> = 3 mA, I<sub>L</sub> = 1 mA and I<sub>Z</sub> = 2 mA.
s3p3.li4: For proper regulation the Zener current must be positive. If the load draws too much current (RL < Rmin), the Zener diode no longer controls the load voltage and the regulator has dropped out of regulation.
s3p3.li5: Line regulation characterizes how sensitive the output voltage is to changes in the input voltage (mV/V); load regulation characterizes how sensitive it is to changes in the load current (Ω). Load regulation is the Thévenin equivalent resistance looking back into the regulator from the load terminals.
s3p3.title: Part 3 · Diode Circuit Analysis

s3p4.cm2: Smaller capacitor, requires center-tapped transformer, two diodes
s3p4.intro: A rectifier converts an ac voltage into a pulsating dc voltage. A filter capacitor then eliminates the ac components of the waveform to produce a nearly constant dc output. Rectifier circuits are used in virtually all electronic devices to convert the ac power line (240 V, 50 Hz in Cyprus) to the dc voltages required for their operation.
s3p4.li1: In rectifier circuits the diode state changes with time, and a given piecewise linear model is valid only for a certain time interval.
s3p4.li2: A step-up or step-down transformer is often used ahead of the rectifier to convert the power-line voltage to the desired ac level.
s3p4.li3: During the positive half-cycle of the input (v<sub>S</sub> = V<sub>P</sub>·sinωt > 0) the diode is on: v<sub>O</sub> = v<sub>S</sub> with the ideal model, or v<sub>O</sub> = v<sub>S</sub> − V<sub>on</sub> with the CVD model.
s3p4.li4: During the negative half-cycle negative current cannot exist in the diode, so it is off. The resistor current is zero and v<sub>O</sub> = 0.
s3p4.li5: Peak detector: with only a capacitor as the load, the capacitor charges up to the peak of the input, the diode cuts off, and with no discharge path the output stays constant: Vdc = VP − Von.
s3p4.li6: RC load: in a real circuit the load resistor slowly discharges the capacitor. When the input exceeds the output again (near the next peak), the diode turns on briefly and recharges the capacitor. The resulting variation in the output is the ripple voltage Vr, the short time the diode conducts is the conduction interval ΔT, and its angular equivalent is the conduction angle θc.
s3p4.ex1: Example: Vrms = 12.6 V (60 Hz), R = 15 Ω, C = 25,000 µF, Von = 1 V. Vdc = 12.6√2 − 1 = 16.8 V, Idc = 16.8/15 = 1.12 A, Vr = 0.747 V, θc = 0.290 rad = 16.6° and ΔT = θc/ω = 0.769 ms. The diode conducts for only 0.77 ms of each 16.7 ms period.
s3p4.li7: Peak diode current IP: all the charge the capacitor supplies to the load in one period (Q = IdcT) is replenished by the diode during the short conduction interval. Modeling the current pulse as a triangle gives Q = IPΔT/2. In the example above IP = 48.6 A.
s3p4.li8: Surge current ISC: when power is first turned on the capacitor is discharged and an even larger current flows, 168 A in the same example. Actual values are smaller because of the neglected series resistances of the diode and transformer.
s3p4.li9: Peak inverse voltage (PIV): when the diode is off the reverse bias across it is Vdc − vS, which reaches about 2VP at the negative peak of the input. The breakdown voltage of the rectifier diode must exceed this value.
s3p4.li10: Power dissipation: the first term comes from the diode voltage drop (1 V × 1.12 A = 1.12 W in the example) and the second from the diode series resistance RS (7.3 W for RS = 0.2 Ω). It can be reduced by minimizing the peak current, using the minimum required filter capacitor or a full-wave rectifier.
s3p4.li11: A full-wave rectifier uses a center-tapped transformer and two diodes to conduct on both half-cycles. The capacitor discharge time is cut in half; all formulas are the same as for the half-wave rectifier with T replaced by T/2, so half the filter capacitance achieves a given ripple voltage.
s3p4.li12: A full-wave bridge rectifier eliminates the center-tapped transformer by using four diodes. Since the current passes through two diodes in each half-cycle, Vdc = VP − 2Von, and the PIV is reduced to VP.
s3p4.li13: Reversing the polarity of the diodes gives the same rectifiers with a negative output voltage.
s3p4.li14: Filter capacitors are a major factor in the cost, size and weight of a rectifier. The cost of the extra diodes is negligible, so the bridge rectifier is usually the preferred choice.
s3p4.ex2: Design example: Vdc = 15 V, Vr < 0.15 V (1% ripple), Idc = 2 A, f = 60 Hz, Von = 1 V. Choosing a bridge rectifier: VP = Vdc + 2Von = 17 V (12 Vrms), C = Idc·(T/2)/Vr = 0.111 F, ΔT = 0.352 ms, IP = Idc·(2/ΔT)·(T/2) = 94.7 A, Isurge = ωCVP = 711 A and PIV = VP = 17 V.

pnSim.title: The pn Junction and Depletion Region
pnSim.lead: Interactive simulation: what does the depletion region do when a voltage is applied to the diode?
pnSim.keyHint: Tip: you can also use the ← → keys to change the voltage in 50 mV steps.
pnSim.clamp: The barrier has almost vanished. Beyond this point the depletion approximation is no longer valid, so a lower limit is shown for the width.
pnSim.note: The simulation uses I<sub>S</sub> = 1 fA, V<sub>T</sub> = 25 mV, n<sub>i</sub> = 10<sup>10</sup> cm<sup>-3</sup> and an example V<sub>Z</sub> = 5 V. The drawing is not to scale; the actual values are listed in the table.
pnSim.tryHint: In each case watch both the cross-section and the ρ(x), E(x), φ(x) plots below it.
pnSim.t1: Move the voltage from 0 toward −5 V. Carriers move away from the junction, the depletion region widens, and E<sub>MAX</sub> and the barrier increase. The current stays at −I<sub>S</sub>: the diode blocks.
pnSim.t2: Slowly raise the voltage to 0.7 V. The barrier drops, the depletion region narrows, and beyond a certain point carriers flow across the junction. Compare the current at 0.60 V and 0.66 V: a factor of 10.
pnSim.t3: Make N<sub>A</sub> and N<sub>D</sub> different. The depletion region extends further into the lightly doped side because the total charge on both sides must be equal: qN<sub>A</sub>x<sub>p</sub> = qN<sub>D</sub>x<sub>n</sub>. Increasing both makes the region narrower and φ<sub>j</sub> larger.
pnSim.t4: Take the voltage below −5 V. The diode enters breakdown and a large reverse current flows. Zener diodes are designed to operate in exactly this region.
